Fourth, we decompose the effect into extensive and\nintensive margins, test host-specificity, and examine adopter-level mechanisms\n(Section~\\ref{sec:decomposition}).\n\n\\subsection{Data}\n\\label{sec:data}\n\n\\paragraph{Concept pool.} We assembled an outcome-blind pool of 426 scientific concepts, where\noutcome-blind means that the inclusion criteria and frame were frozen and SHA-256-hashed before any\npost-appearance data were inspected. Concepts are noun-phrase surface forms that first appeared in\nOpenAlex~\\citep{Priem2022} titles and abstracts between 2005 and 2016, with 20 to 300 papers in the\nfirst-appearance window and no more than 8,000 total works through 2024.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-1/dataset-1}.}\nOf the 426, 366 are main emerging concepts (247 Screen, 119 Held-out, split by a SHA-1 hash on concept\nidentifiers) and 60 are stationary reference concepts. A logistic-regression classifier trained on\nsilver-standard labels (F1 $= 0.82$ on 300 test items, AUC $= 0.89$) and a variant merger (B-cubed\nF1 $= 0.78$) were applied to ground every concept.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-1}.}\nThe pool is dominated by physics, physical-sciences and computer-science concepts sourced from arXiv.\nFor the Screen fold, 202 concepts survive grounding filters; for the Held-out fold, 100.\n\n\\paragraph{MeSH check population.} An independent biomedical arm of 191 concepts was drawn from new MeSH\ndescriptors (DateEstablished 2006 to 2016, widened to 2004--2005 and 2017--2018), surviving a provenance\nfilter, a PubMed novelty pre-screen and the same early-volume rule. Only approximately 25\\% of new MeSH\ndescriptors are genuinely new concepts; the remainder are reclassifications or splits.\n\n\\paragraph{Works.} The combined corpus comprises 462,812 unique OpenAlex works with 488,078 verified\nconcept--work links, spanning 2000 to 2024.\n\n\\paragraph{Co-word network.} From a design-weighted whole-science background sample of 259,716 works, we\nbuilt 25 yearly three-year-window co-occurrence snapshots (approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges per\nsnapshot), with association-strength edge weights~\\citep{vanEck2009}, Leiden community\ndetection~\\citep{Traag2018} (best of five seeds) and alluvial community identifiers.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-3}.}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-nativeness profiles.} For each concept-keyword node, we retrieved exact OpenAlex\nsubfield-by-time-block publication counts, covering 78.7\\% of host co-occurrence weight across 1,372 nodes.\nThese profiles supply the host-vocabulary share used in RQ2. Figure~\\ref{fig:network} shows a schematic of the\nresulting network.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig2_v0.jpg}\n  \\caption{Schematic illustration of the co-word network structure. Nodes represent concept-keyword terms\n  and grey edges represent co-occurrence links; node fill colour marks Leiden community\n  membership, and larger circles are high-degree hub terms. Background terms (plain nodes) form dense\n  communities joined by a few inter-community edges. Pool concepts (bold black rings) sit on the periphery\n  of communities, mostly in the gaps between two of them, where they act as bridge or connector nodes; three\n  are labelled as examples (\\emph{wireless backhaul}, \\emph{EPR steering}, \\emph{holographic QCD}); their\n  placement in the diagram is illustrative and does not reflect their actual network coordinates. The full\n  network comprises approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges; the panel is a schematic rendering\n  for readability and does not depict a specific yearly snapshot.}\n  \\label{fig:network}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Structural precursors of emergence}\n\\label{sec:rq1method}\n\n\\paragraph{Emergence labels.} The pre-declared emergence label required a concept-year reaching at least 20\npapers per year and gaining at least 20 percentile points in co-word network strength. Because pool concepts sit\nin the bottom few percent of network strength, it produced only 4 onsets, so a sustained-uptake label\n($E_{\\mathrm{up}}$) was promoted after that result was seen; $E_{\\mathrm{up}}$ is therefore a post-hoc label, and\nevery RQ1 result below uses it. Its held-out test was then specified and frozen before the held-out fold was\nopened.\n\n\\paragraph{Matched event study.} For each concept showing sustained uptake, we matched it to a control concept\nfrom the same first-appearance band and origin field that did not show sustained uptake, using 1:1\nnearest-neighbour matching on pre-period network indicators. The standardised mean difference between treated\nand control concepts at lags $k = -3$ to $0$ is the event-study estimand. A pooled panel regression of\nthe binary future-emergence indicator on the closure measure provides a second estimand, reported as the panel\ncoefficient. Bootstrap confidence intervals ($B = 2{,}000$) and Holm-corrected $p$-values control for multiple\ntesting. The Screen fold (202 concepts) produced 68 onsets and 26 matched pairs.\n\n\\paragraph{Closure measures.} To test whether pre-emergence closure is reducible to neighbourhood turnover\nor Burt brokerage, we computed four variants: (a) turnover-residualised closure, obtained by regressing\nclosure on the new-relation rate, novelty, Baselga beta-similarity, log volume, concept age and Shannon\nentropy; (b) persistent-neighbour closure, restricting the closure coefficient to the top-20 neighbours\npresent in both year $y$ and $y{-}1$; (c) Burt constraint and effective size of the weighted ego\nnetwork~\\citep{Burt2004}; and (d) cross-community pair excess, defined as the count of partner pairs from\ndistinct Leiden communities minus the count expected under a strength-decile null.\n\n\\subsection{Host-entry grafting}\n\\label{sec:rq2method}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-entry events.} A host-entry event is the first year in which a concept appears in a\nnon-origin subfield together with at least five co-occurring partner terms. From 4,177 main-arm host entries,\nthe Screen fold retains 1,544 events across 140 concept clusters after the partner-count filter.\n\n\\paragraph{Exposure variable.} Host-vocabulary share is the tag-weighted mean of each partner's pre-entry\npublication share in the host subfield, where tag-weighted means that each co-occurrence edge is weighted by\nits association strength. The continuous measure is primary because only 1.1\\% of partner tags have a host\nshare above 50\\%. Co-transfer is the fraction of partners that were origin companions of the concept in the\nfive years before entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Outcome.} Five-year newcomer uptake: the count of host-subfield papers by author-disjoint newcomers\n(authors with no prior concept paper and no co-authorship with concept authors) during the five years after entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Model.} Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood (PPML) regression~\\citep{Silva2006} with\nconcept-clustered standard errors~\\citep{Cameron2015}. Two specifications were pre-registered. The primary\nspecification includes concept-by-entry-year and host-by-entry-year fixed effects. The co-primary specification\nincludes concept, entry-year and host fixed effects; a pre-declared thin-cell rule makes it co-primary when the\nprimary specification retains less than 30\\% of events or fewer than 50 concept clusters, which happened on the\nScreen fold (the primary retained 26\\% of events, 77 clusters). Both specifications include co-transfer as a second\nregressor.\n\n\\paragraph{Held-out fold.} 93 concepts, 1,100 entries; minimum detectable effect (co-primary): IRR per\nstandard deviation of 1.15. Its entry events and pre-entry (W1) features were computed before any outcome was\nread, but its outcomes stayed sealed under a hash-checked specification until they were opened once, with a\nlock file, after the screen analysis was frozen.\n\n\\paragraph{MeSH replication.} The same analysis was applied to 191 MeSH concepts under a frozen specification.\nThe declared design (at least five partners and nativeness coverage of at least 0.50) yielded only 192 events in\n46 non-singleton concepts, so the pre-declared widening (at least three partners, coverage 0.30) fired before\noutcomes were read, producing 2,171 co-primary events across 160 concept clusters. Entries into non-biomedical\nhosts are dropped, so the replication covers biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries only.\n\n\\subsection{Post-confirmation decomposition}\n\\label{sec:decomposition}\n\nAfter the Held-out and MeSH tests confirmed the host-vocabulary effect, three decompositions were\nspecified and frozen before any coefficient was read; because every fold had already been opened, they are\npost-confirmation exploratory:\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n\\item \\textbf{Extensive versus intensive margins.} A linear probability model for whether any newcomer uptake\noccurs (extensive margin), and PPML conditional on uptake having started (intensive margin). Inverse-variance\nweighting (IVW) pools estimates across the Screen, Held-out and MeSH folds.\n\n\\item \\textbf{Host-specific versus generic accessibility.} Generality proxies (tag-weighted normalised subfield\nentropy and log block frequency of each partner) are added as controls. The Balassa-index lift\nmeasure~\\citep{Balassa1965}, defined as the log ratio of the host-vocabulary share to the partner's baseline\nsubfield share, is tested as an alternative exposure variable.\n\n\\item \\textbf{Origin-field dependence.} A Wald test of equality across origin-field groups (Physics and\nAstronomy, Computer Science, other).\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{RQ1: Structural precursors of emergence}\n\\label{sec:rq1}\n\n\\subsubsection{Experimental setup}\n\\label{sec:rq1_setup}\n\nThe Screen fold (202 concepts) produced 68 onsets of sustained uptake and 26 matched concept pairs after 1:1\nnearest-neighbour matching on pre-period network indicators. The Held-out fold produced 30 onsets and 22\nmatched pairs; because the Held-out fold's own never-treated pool was too small (33 concepts), 17 of 25 unique\ncontrols were drawn from the Screen fold's never-treated pool, so the Held-out estimator is not fully\ncontrol-side independent.\n\n\\subsubsection{Results}\n\\label{sec:rq1_results}\n\nOn the Screen fold, concepts that later show sustained uptake have lower general closure in the years before\nonset (matched event-study standardised mean difference $= -0.44$, 95\\% CI $[-0.81, -0.05]$; panel\ncoefficient $= -0.66$). The pre-registered positive sign was not observed; the effect runs in the opposite\ndirection.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Closure on the sealed held-out fold. ``Screen panel'' is the panel coefficient on\nthe Screen fold. ``HO panel'' and ``HO event-study'' are the panel coefficient and matched event-study\nstandardised mean difference on the Held-out fold. Holm-corrected $p$-values apply to the panel coefficient.}\n\\label{tab:closure}\n\\footnotesize\n\\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{X c c c c l}\n\\toprule\nMeasure & Screen panel & HO panel & HO event-study [95\\% CI] & Holm $p$ & Status \\\\\n\\midrule\nGeneral closure & $-0.66$ & $-0.39$ & $-0.53\\;[-1.20, +0.07]$ & 0.147 & Not confirmed \\\\\nTurnover-resid. & $-0.40$ & $-0.11$ & $-0.27\\;[-0.89, +0.30]$ & 0.635 & Not confirmed \\\\\nPersistent-neighbour & $-1.12$ & $-1.07$ & $-0.83\\;[-1.71, -0.10]$ & 0.015 & Confirmed \\\\\nBurt constraint & $+0.06$ & $+0.08$ & $+0.11\\;[+0.02, +0.19]$ & --- & Positive \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\multicolumn{6}{l}{\\scriptsize HO = Held-out fold. Holm $p$ tests the panel coefficient.}\n\\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:closure} and Figure~\\ref{fig:closure} summarise these results. On the sealed held-out fold,\ngeneral closure is not significant (Holm $p = 0.147$), and the frozen kill mapping returns R1\\_DEAD:\nstructural precursors of sustained uptake are volume/churn correlates. Only persistent-neighbour closure, restricted to top-20 neighbours present in consecutive\nyears, is significant: the panel coefficient is $-1.07$ (Holm $p = 0.015$) and the matched event-study\nstandardised mean difference is $-0.83$ (95\\% CI $[-1.71, -0.10]$). Burt constraint has the same positive\nsign on the Held-out fold (event-study $+0.11$, 95\\% CI $[0.02, 0.19]$), indicating that the lower closure\nbefore emergence is not Burt brokerage: concepts that later emerge sit in ego networks that are more\nconstrained, not less (effective size is also lower on held-out, $-27.8$, 95\\% CI $[-49.3, -9.5]$). The\npersistent-neighbour row carries three caveats: its screen event-study interval included zero ($-0.58$,\n95\\% CI $[-1.27, 0.12]$), 17 of the 25 held-out controls are screen concepts, and covariate balance is poor\n(entropy standardised mean difference 0.96; 6 of 11 covariates above 0.25).\n\nThe MeSH replication is directional under a sensitivity label (standardised mean difference $D = -0.42$, Holm $p = 0.039$, $n = 29$),\nsame sign as the main pool, but under the primary label the MeSH effect is null ($D = -0.09$, Holm\n$p = 0.677$, $n = 15$).%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-4}.}\n\nStructural precursors add no predictive value for whether a concept will later show sustained uptake beyond\nfrequency, burst, degree and entropy baselines (logistic AUC 0.89 versus 0.88, delta $-0.010$, 95\\% CI\n$-0.045$ to 0.021).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig3_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Pre-emergence closure on the held-out fold, by measure type. Each row shows the standardised mean\n  difference between concepts that later show sustained uptake and matched controls. Points are estimates\n  and horizontal bars are 95\\% bootstrap confidence intervals. The dashed vertical line marks no effect,\n  and Holm-corrected $p$-values are listed to the right of the first three rows. Only\n  persistent-neighbour closure (blue) survives Holm correction (event-study $-0.83$, 95\\% CI\n  $[-1.71, -0.10]$; panel coefficient $-1.07$, Holm $p = 0.015$). General closure\n  (Holm $p = 0.147$) and turnover-residualised closure (Holm $p = 0.635$) are shown in grey: they do not\n  survive confirmation, and their intervals cross zero. Burt constraint (orange) is positive ($+0.11$,\n  95\\% CI $[0.02, 0.19]$), which indicates that emerging concepts sit in more constrained, not more\n  brokered, ego networks.}\n  \\label{fig:closure}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsubsection{Comparison to related work}\n\\label{sec:rq1_comparison}\n\nThe finding that emerging concepts show lower closure among their most stable co-word neighbours is consistent\nwith the work of \\citet{Salatino2017}, who found that new topics tend to emerge where weakly interconnected\nresearch areas begin to cross-fertilise, and with \\citeauthor{Chen2009}'s~\\citeyearpar{Chen2009} theory of structural variation\nin which transformative work bridges structural holes. It is also consistent with the structural-holes\nliterature~\\citep{Burt2004}: concepts that later emerge connect across Leiden communities, and their\ncross-community pair excess is positive. The critical difference is that Burt constraint is higher, not lower.\nIn Burt's framework, brokerage means low constraint. Here the ego network is more redundant, not less, so an\nincreasing-brokerage pathway is ruled out for these concepts. The pre-registered reading that openness is\nconfined to the top of an otherwise dense neighbourhood was tested on held-out and is not supported, because\nthe closure component was not confirmed. This pattern is\ncloser to what \\citet{Lin2022} describe as disconnection and discordance enabling new directions in science,\nand to \\citeauthor{Larson2017}'s~\\citeyearpar{Larson2017} finding that weak-tie diffusion in networks is not\nguaranteed to carry novel information.\n\nAmong Applied Network Science contributions, \\citet{Domenico2016} studied knowledge diaspora through\nsource-sink author flows, and \\citet{Cunningham2022} built field-of-study networks that link topics through the\nauthors who publish in them and used structural role analysis to characterise the multidisciplinary roles of\ntopics. Our analysis works at the level of concept co-word neighbourhoods rather than author-defined topic\nnetworks. \\citet{Fontaine2024} traced the penetration of AI into neuroscience and found epistemic integration\nalongside social segregation: AI research formed a distinct, socially confined ecosystem inside the field, a\ncase of presence in a field that differs from integration into it. \\citet{Doonan2019} found that community structure in co-inventor networks affects\ntime to first citation, paralleling our finding that community position shapes concept uptake.\n\n\\subsubsection{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:rq1_discussion}\n\nUnder the pre-registered kill rule, RQ1 is answered negatively: structural precursors of sustained uptake are\nvolume/churn correlates, and they add nothing to frequency, burst, degree and entropy baselines in prediction.\nThe qualification is the persistent-neighbour closure row: concepts whose top associates do not close into\ntriads from year to year are more likely to show sustained uptake on the held-out fold. It is a single row,\nits screen event-study interval included zero, and the held-out matching falls back to Screen controls for\n17 of 25 unique controls, so we treat it as a lead rather than a finding. Burt constraint is positive, meaning\nthe ego network is redundant, not brokered; brokerage across a structural hole is ruled out as the pathway.\n\n\\subsection{RQ2: Host-entry grafting}\n\\label{sec:rq2}\n\n\\subsubsection{Experimental setup}\n\\label{sec:rq2_setup}\n\nThe host-entry sample for the Screen fold comprises 1,544 events across 140 concept clusters (co-primary\nspecification). Entry is predominantly a package: 70\\% of partner tags are non-native origin companions, and\nonly 1.8\\% are native grafts (host share above 50\\%). The mean host-vocabulary share is 0.043 (SD 0.055). The\nHeld-out fold has 972 events across 74 concept clusters. The MeSH population has 2,171 events across 160\nconcept clusters.\n\n\\subsubsection{Results}\n\\label{sec:rq2_results}\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Host-entry grafting: pre-registered test. IRR/SD = incidence-rate ratio per one standard deviation\nof host-vocabulary share. CT = co-transfer. G = concept clusters. IVW = inverse-variance weighted pool of the Screen and MeSH\nco-primary estimates. The Screen primary row has Holm $p = 0.15$.}\n\\label{tab:grafting}\n\\small\n\\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{l l c c c c c c}\n\\toprule\nSpecification & Fold & IRR/SD & 95\\% CI & $p$ & CT $p$ & $N$ & $G$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nCo-primary & Screen & 1.30 & 1.16--1.45 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & 0.48 & 1,544 & 140 \\\\\nCo-primary & Held-out & 1.19 & 1.06--1.33 & 0.004 & 0.60 & 972 & 74 \\\\\nPrimary (strict FE) & Held-out & 0.98 & 0.70--1.37 & 0.91 & 0.22 & 250 & 30 \\\\\nCo-primary & MeSH & 1.23 & 1.12--1.36 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & 0.053 & 2,171 & 160 \\\\\nPrimary & MeSH & 1.32 & 1.10--1.60 & 0.004 & 0.46 & 1,004 & 122 \\\\\nPrimary (strict FE) & Screen & 1.39 & 0.97--1.99 & 0.074 & 0.85 & 452 & 77 \\\\\nCo-primary (IVW) & Screen + MeSH & 1.26 & 1.17--1.36 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & --- & --- & --- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:grafting} presents the pre-registered test. On the Screen fold, a one-standard-deviation\nincrease in host-vocabulary share raises newcomer uptake by 30\\% (co-primary IRR 1.30, 95\\% CI 1.16 to 1.45).\nOn the sealed held-out fold, opened once, the co-primary IRR is 1.19 (95\\% CI 1.06 to 1.33; Holm $p = 0.009$,\nwild-cluster bootstrap $p = 0.012$, nativeness-permutation $p = 0.026$, placebo-calibrated $p = 0.034$;\na within-concept shuffle permutation gives a borderline $p = 0.050$), so the pre-declared kill rule is not\ntriggered. Heterogeneity between Screen and Held-out is not significant ($p = 0.25$). On the MeSH biomedical\npopulation the co-primary IRR is 1.23 (95\\% CI 1.12 to 1.36, $p < 0.001$; primary IRR 1.32, 95\\% CI 1.10 to\n1.60, $p = 0.004$; pre-registered verdict: REPLICATED for biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries). The\ninverse-variance weighted pool of the Screen and MeSH co-primary estimates is 1.26 (95\\% CI 1.17\nto 1.36, $I^2 = 0$). Co-transfer is null across all folds and specifications\n(Figure~\\ref{fig:grafting}).\n\nThe fully saturated primary specification on the Held-out fold is inconclusive (IRR 0.98, 95\\% CI 0.70 to\n1.37) because it retains only 250 of 972 events with 30 concept clusters; this was declared underpowered in\nadvance (minimum detectable effect IRR 1.30).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig4_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Host-vocabulary effect on five-year newcomer uptake across folds and specifications. Each row gives\n  the PPML incidence-rate ratio (IRR) per one standard deviation of host-vocabulary share, on a log axis;\n  horizontal bars are 95\\% concept-clustered confidence intervals, and the dashed vertical line marks\n  IRR $= 1$ (no effect). Filled circles are the co-primary specification (concept, entry-year and host fixed\n  effects) and open circles the primary specification with concept$\\times$year and host$\\times$year fixed\n  effects. Blue marks the OpenAlex screen and sealed held-out folds, green the independent MeSH replication,\n  and the amber diamond the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) pooled co-primary estimate. The co-primary effect\n  is significant on all three folds (screen IRR 1.30 [1.16, 1.45], held-out 1.19 [1.06, 1.33], MeSH 1.23\n  [1.12, 1.36]), and the pooled estimate is 1.26 [1.17, 1.36] (Screen and MeSH co-primary). The primary specification is inconclusive on\n  the held-out fold (IRR 0.98 [0.70, 1.37], 30 clusters, $p = 0.91$) but significant on MeSH (IRR 1.32\n  [1.10, 1.60]). Grey diamonds are the co-transfer regressor from the co-primary models. Its intervals\n  include 1 on every fold ($p = 0.48$, $0.60$ and $0.053$). The right-hand columns list each estimate with\n  its 95\\% CI and $p$-value.}\n  \\label{fig:grafting}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Robustness.} The co-primary effect holds in 20 of 26 robustness variants on the Screen fold\nincluding the base row and field strata, and in 18 of 22 excluding them (IRR range 1.11 to 1.56 among\nsignificant rows); binary nativeness cut-offs at 0.5 and 0.7 are null. All seven pre-specified robustness rows on the Held-out fold are\nsignificant. Nativeness-permutation placebos are centred on 1.0 (co-primary $p = 0.002$ Screen, 0.026\nHeld-out, 0.010 MeSH). The cluster-robust variance estimator mildly over-rejects at the null (size 10.5\\% on\nMeSH simulation), so $p$-values should be read alongside the wild-cluster and permutation results.\n\n\\subsubsection{Mechanism decomposition}\n\\label{sec:rq2_mechanism}\n\n\\paragraph{Extensive versus intensive margins.} The host-vocabulary effect operates through both the extensive\nmargin, meaning whether any newcomer uptake starts, and the intensive margin, meaning the count of newcomer\npapers given that uptake started. The inverse-variance weighted extensive-margin effect is $+6.4$ percentage\npoints per standard deviation (95\\% CI 4.8 to 8.1, randomisation-$t$ $p < 0.001$), approximately a 13\\%\nincrease relative to the base rate of 51\\%. The inverse-variance weighted intensive-margin incidence-rate ratio\nper standard deviation is 1.18 (95\\% CI 1.10 to 1.27). The extensive share of the total effect is 0.38\n(95\\% CI 0.21 to 0.55; Figure~\\ref{fig:margins}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig5_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Decomposition of the host-vocabulary effect into extensive and intensive margins across the screen,\n  held-out and MeSH folds. Blue circles show per-fold estimates, vermillion diamonds the inverse-variance-weighted\n  (IVW) pooled estimate, and horizontal bars 95\\% confidence intervals. (a)~Extensive margin:\n  linear-probability-model effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in host-vocabulary share on the\n  probability of any newcomer uptake, in percentage points per SD (dashed line: no effect). The pooled effect\n  is 6.43~pp (95\\% CI 4.76 to 8.11). (b)~Intensive margin: PPML incidence-rate ratio per SD conditional on\n  uptake, on a log axis (dashed line: IRR $= 1$). The pooled IRR is 1.183 (95\\% CI 1.104 to 1.267). All three\n  folds are positive on both margins, and every fold interval excludes the null. (c)~Share of the total effect:\n  the extensive margin accounts for 38\\% (95\\% CI 21\\% to 55\\%, black whisker) and the intensive margin for\n  the remaining 62\\%.}\n  \\label{fig:margins}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-specific versus generic accessibility.} Adding generality controls (subfield entropy and log\nfrequency of entry partners) to the co-primary model retains 97\\% of the host-vocabulary coefficient\n(inverse-variance weighted retention 0.97, 95\\% CI 0.81 to 1.10), and the Balassa-index lift measure is also\nsignificant (inverse-variance weighted IRR per standard deviation 1.34, 95\\% CI 1.23 to 1.46). The\nhost-vocabulary gradient is not reducible to generic concept accessibility. However, within fixed effects the\nBalassa-index lift measure has a correlation of 0.997 with the log of the continuous host-vocabulary share,\nso the lift leg of this test is weak: the two measures carry nearly the same within-unit information, and the\nlift result should be interpreted as confirming the continuous share rather than adding independent evidence\nfor host-specificity.\n\n\\paragraph{No origin-field boundary.} The Wald test for equality of the host-vocabulary effect across\norigin-field groups (Physics and Astronomy, Computer Science, other) is null ($p = 0.64$, label-permutation\n$p = 0.77$). Physics and Astronomy concepts, whose host-vocabulary coefficient is individually non-significant\n(IRR 1.18, 95\\% CI 0.93 to 1.50), fall within sampling variation of the other groups.\n\n\\subsubsection{Diffusion typology and expansion-before-diffusion ordering}\n\\label{sec:rq2_typology}\n\nA data-derived typology based on multivariate dynamic time warping of three diversity channels (rarefied\nShannon entropy, Rao-Stirling diversity~\\citep{Stirling2007} and active subfield count) yields a stable\ntwo-cluster solution ($k$-medoids, Hennig bootstrap~\\citep{Hennig2007} minimum Jaccard 0.86):\n\\textbf{localised} ($n = 136$, low entropy and few active subfields) and \\textbf{broad from the start}\n($n = 66$, high entropy from early years). Finer clusterings are unstable ($k = 3$ Jaccard 0.60). The typology\ndoes not separate outcomes better than an entropy-only baseline after residualising on early volume.\n\nCrossing the typology with rooting separates occupancy from rooting. On the Screen fold, broad-from-the-start\nconcepts have almost three times as many host entries per concept as localised ones (18.4 versus 6.6) and a\nhigher establishment rate (0.31 versus 0.13). Their raw host-vocabulary share is lower, and after host-by-year\nfixed effects and relatedness density the gap is null on both folds (Screen $-0.0018$; Held-out $+0.0005$,\n95\\% CI $-0.010$ to 0.011), so the pre-declared prediction that broad concepts arrive with more host vocabulary\nfails. Their co-transfer is lower (Held-out $-0.125$, 95\\% CI $-0.19$ to $-0.06$): broadly integrated concepts\ntravel less as packages. Within each type, host-vocabulary share predicts newcomer uptake (Screen PPML IRR per SD\n1.36 for broad and 1.16 for localised concepts; interaction $p = 0.11$, exploratory). The typology measures where\na concept is present; host-vocabulary share measures whether it is taken up there.\n\nAmong concepts exhibiting both a co-word-network expansion onset and a disciplinary-diffusion onset, expansion\nprecedes diffusion in 25 of 26 pooled main-arm cases (proportion 0.96, bootstrap 95\\% CI 0.88 to 1.00; on the\nScreen fold alone 15 of 16 against a year-shuffle null of 0.62, $p = 0.004$), but only 8.6\\% of concepts have\nboth onsets observable. This ordering holds only conditionally: diffusion onsets are rarer overall (log-rank\n$p = 0.005$), the evaluability rule favours this order, the cohort first seen by 2012 has only 12 dual-onset\nconcepts, and the Granger panel coefficient is negative and not significant ($b = -0.0013$, $p = 0.068$). On\nMeSH, 9 of 13 show expansion first (not different from the null, $p = 0.43$).\n\n\\subsubsection{Adopter-level mechanism}\n\\label{sec:rq2_adopter}\n\nAdopters, defined as author-disjoint newcomers who publish a concept paper in the host subfield within the\nfive-year outcome window, are more likely to have prior corpus exposure to the concept's entry partners than matched non-adopters\nfrom the same host subfield (conditional logistic regression: OR 3.09; prevalence 0.79 versus 0.61; 95\\% CI\n2.32 to 4.28; 1,013 matched strata, 422 entries, 109 concepts). Exposure to frequency-matched\nnegative-control concepts is negatively associated (OR 0.62), and the placebo control using partners of a\ndifferent concept's entry into the same host is also below 1 (OR 0.72), showing specificity to the concept's\nown partners. Exposure is measured only within the corpus: 87\\% of the 21,941 adopter pairs have no prior corpus\nwork and are excluded.\n\nDecomposing partners into three vocabulary classes --- FOREIGN (origin vocabulary, host share below 5\\%),\nADJACENT (5\\% to 30\\%) and NATIVE (host vocabulary, above 30\\%) --- enrichment follows a gradient: FOREIGN\npartners OR 2.88, ADJACENT partners OR 1.91, NATIVE partners OR 1.47. Adopters who pick up a concept in a new\nfield are most enriched for prior exposure to its origin-vocabulary partners. This is consistent with the\nabsorptive-capacity framework~\\citep{Cohen1990}, in which recognising external knowledge depends on prior\nfamiliarity with it, and equally with plain topical proximity of adopters to the concept. Enrichment does not\ninteract with host-vocabulary share (OR 0.87, 95\\% CI 0.70 to 1.14), and the pre-exposed adopter pool does not\nmediate the entry-level effect (attenuation 0.05, 95\\% CI $-0.08$ to 0.23). This Screen-fold result is not\nindependently confirmed.\n\n\\subsubsection{Representative cases}\n\\label{sec:rq2_cases}\n\nFour medoid cases from the typology clusters illustrate the host-vocabulary gradient at the concept level\n(Figure~\\ref{fig:cases}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig6_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Four representative cases of the host-vocabulary gradient. Each panel shows one concept, and each\n  horizontal bar is one of its host entries in the co-primary sample, labelled by host subfield and entry year\n  and sorted by host-vocabulary share (x-axis, fraction). Green bars are rooted entries and grey bars are\n  non-rooted entries. The dashed line marks the mean share of the non-rooted entries, and rooted bars are\n  annotated with their share and number of newcomer papers. (a)~Wireless backhaul (broad, CS): 14 entries, one\n  rooted (Aerospace Engineering 2008, share 0.084, 6 newcomers) against a non-rooted mean of 0.021.\n  (b)~Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen (EPR) steering (broad, Physics): 7 entries, one rooted (Artificial Intelligence\n  2011, 0.142, 37 newcomers; co-transfer 0) against a non-rooted mean of 0.027. (c)~Locally repairable code\n  (localised, CS): a single co-primary entry, rooted (0.056, 3 newcomers), so there is no within-concept\n  contrast. (d)~Holographic QCD (localised, Physics): 5 entries, none rooted (mean 0.041; three have\n  co-transfer 1.0), including an AMO Physics entry at 0.132 that did not take root. In (a) and (b), the rooted\n  entry has a higher host-vocabulary share than every non-rooted entry of the same concept. The panels are\n  descriptive, so no intervals are drawn.}\n  \\label{fig:cases}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Wireless backhaul} (broad type, Computer Science, first appeared 2006). Broad from its first year,\nsplitting between Computer Networks and Electrical Engineering. By 2022 seven subfields are active. Of 14 host\nentries in the co-primary sample, only one is rooted (Aerospace Engineering in 2008, host-vocabulary share\n0.084, 6 newcomer papers). The 13 non-rooted entries average a host-vocabulary share of 0.021 and arrive as\norigin packages (co-transfer 0.6 to 1.0). Rooted-minus-unrooted host-vocabulary share: $+0.062$.\n\n\\paragraph{Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen steering} (broad type, Physics, first appeared 2011). Of 7 co-primary\nentries, one is rooted. The rooted entry's host subfield is labelled ``Artificial Intelligence'' in the\nOpenAlex subfield taxonomy; this placement arises because OpenAlex files the topic ``Quantum Information\nand Cryptography'' under its Artificial Intelligence subfield, which is broader than the colloquial meaning\nof AI. The rooted entry has host-vocabulary share 0.142, co-transfer 0,\nand 37 newcomer papers. The 6 non-rooted entries average 0.027 with co-transfer at or above 0.55.\nRooted-minus-unrooted: $+0.115$. A broad-type label can hide a concept whose cross-disciplinary integration\nrests on a single well-anchored entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Locally repairable code} (localised type, Computer Science, first appeared 2013). Stays at 84\\% to\n96\\% in Computer Networks for its life. Has only 1 co-primary entry. The host subfield for this entry is\nlabelled ``Artificial Intelligence'' in the OpenAlex taxonomy, because OpenAlex files the relevant topic under\nits AI subfield, following the same broad assignment noted above.\nHost-vocabulary share 0.056, rooted. Demonstrates rooting without broad occupancy.\n\n\\paragraph{Holographic QCD} (localised type, Physics, first appeared 2006). Stays at 95\\% to 97\\% in Nuclear\nand High Energy Physics. Its 5 co-primary entries are all non-rooted, averaging 0.041, with three having\nco-transfer of 1.0: pure origin packages. No entry is rooted. A locally concentrated concept whose excursions\nare packaged imports that do not take root.\n\n\\subsubsection{Comparison to related work}\n\\label{sec:rq2_comparison}\n\nOur host-vocabulary measure is closest to the ideational embeddedness of \\citet{Cheng2023}, who found that a\nconcept's fit with existing traditions raises its yearly article count. Their measure is a global property of\nthe concept (mean cosine similarity of all its neighbours in a word2vec embedding), whereas ours is\nentry-specific: measured at the level of each concept-subfield-year event, with concept and host fixed effects\nabsorbing concept-level confounds. Co-transfer, the natural competitor, is null. This extends the principle\nthat relatedness predicts diversification, documented in economic\ngeography~\\citep{Boschma2014, Hidalgo2018}, to the level of individual concept-entry events.\n\nAmong Applied Network Science papers, our work engages most directly with the source-sink analysis of\nknowledge diaspora by \\citet{Domenico2016}, which modelled author flows as diffusion on a bipartite field\nnetwork. Our approach measures concept-vocabulary composition at the entry point rather than author flows; we do\nnot compare the two channels. \\citet{Cunningham2022} characterised the multidisciplinary roles of topics in\nauthor-defined field-of-study networks. \\citet{Fontaine2024} found that AI entered neuroscience epistemically\nwhile its practitioners stayed socially segregated; our distinction between occupying a subfield and being\ntaken up by its own newcomers is in the same spirit. \\citet{Holmgren2023} developed multilevel alluvial methods for mapping\nchange in higher-order networks, related to the alluvial community tracking we use. \\citet{Medeuov2021}\ncompared semantic networks through concept-centred ego subnetworks, the same ego-level view that underlies our\nclosure and constraint measures.\n\\citet{Larson2017} showed that weak ties do not guarantee novel information diffusion, complementing our\nfinding that the vocabulary composition of entry partners, not merely the structural position, predicts rooting.\n\\citet{Doonan2019} found that co-inventor community structure affects time to first citation, providing\na parallel at the patent level to our concept-uptake results. \\citet{Cai2025} examined how knowledge-graph\nextraction errors propagate into downstream network analyses, an issue relevant to the OpenAlex concept\nassignments on which our co-word network is built.\n\n\\subsubsection{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:rq2_discussion}\n\nThe central finding is that a concept's first partners in a new subfield carry information about whether that\nconcept will subsequently be adopted by newcomer scientists in the host field. The host-vocabulary share\npredicts five-year newcomer uptake in a pre-registered design, confirmed on a sealed held-out fold and\nreplicated for biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries in a MeSH population. The effect is graded and on the count\nof newcomer papers; it does not predict a binary establishment threshold on the held-out fold.\n\nThe entry-level and adopter-level results are two separate channels, and we do not merge them into one\nmechanism. At the entry level, host-leaning vocabulary goes with more newcomer uptake. At the adopter level, the\nindividuals who pick up the concept are enriched for prior exposure to the concept's origin-vocabulary partners\n(OR 3.09; prevalence 0.79 vs.\\ 0.61; Screen fold, not independently confirmed), which is consistent with\nabsorptive capacity~\\citep{Cohen1990} or with topical proximity. Host-leaning entries do not raise uptake by\nenlarging this pre-exposed pool: the pool does not mediate the entry-level effect.\n\n\\subsection{Community roles and bridging}\n\\label{sec:community}\n\nLeiden community roles (five-seed agreement 97.2\\%) partition concepts into four categories: bridge (0.61),\nother (0.33), stayer (0.03) and migrant (0.02). Emerging concepts are peripheral or connector nodes in the\nGuimera--Amaral cartography~\\citep{Guimera2005a} (peripheral 0.49, connector 0.40, kinless 0.10, no hubs).\nLagged roles do not robustly predict host-subfield entry (bridge odds ratio 0.64, 95\\% CI 0.38 to 1.08).\n\nMost emerging concepts act as bridges between Leiden communities in the co-word network (early-bridging share\n0.70 in the main pool versus 0.59 in MeSH, difference $+0.11$, 95\\% CI 0.02 to 0.20), but this bridging role\nis common and non-discriminating.\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\subsection{Null findings and what they bound}\n\nFigure~\\ref{fig:decision} places every test on the pre-registered decision path, with failed gates and null or\ndead tests kept in grey rather than dropped. Several pre-registered hypotheses were not supported. Co-transfer, defined as arriving with origin companions,\nis null in all specifications and populations, meaning that the composition of entry matters but the\nimported-package channel does not. The breadth-prediction screen (does openness predict how many new subfields\na concept will reach?) found no effect beyond growth and level baselines.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/experiment-6}.}\nThe link between pre-emergence closure and later host-entry composition is null (partial correlation 0.025\nScreen, 0.053 Held-out, both confidence intervals including zero), meaning that network openness and vocabulary\ncomposition operate independently rather than through a shared mechanism.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=0.88\\linewidth,height=0.66\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig7_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Population flow and pre-registered decision path (layout and numbers from the run's figure registry). (1)~Data and\n  grounding: 426 candidate concepts (366 emerging, 60 reference), 462,812 works, the sealed fold split (screen 202\n  and held-out 100 main concepts) and the 191-concept MeSH pool. (2)~The two network views. (3)~Decision path:\n  the source-sink viability hypothesis and Gate~A failed, so the pre-declared host-entry grafting test took over;\n  it was screened (1,544 events, 140 concepts), confirmed on the sealed held-out fold (972 events, 74 concepts) and\n  replicated in MeSH for biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries (2,171 events, 160 concepts), and the adopter test is\n  mechanism evidence on the screen fold. Grey dashed boxes are dead or null: openness predicting breadth, co-transfer,\n  the link from early closure to later host-vocabulary share, and RQ1 structural precursors, which the\n  held-out test declared dead. (4)~The RQ2 descriptive layer (the lead-lag share shown is the screen fold's 15 of\n  16). Construct definitions are given in Section~\\ref{sec:methods}.}\n  \\label{fig:decision}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\n\\paragraph{What the held-out fold does and does not protect.} The held-out fold's outcomes were sealed and\nopened once, but its entry events, pre-entry features and population size were computed on the same pipeline\nbefore opening, and an early experiment computed origin-series summaries for 61 of its concepts. The\nconfirmation therefore guards against outcome-driven choices, not against every choice of frame. The MeSH\npopulation is not wholly unseen either: it was used for the RQ1 replication before the grafting test.\n\n\\paragraph{Population bias.} The concept pool is dominated by physics, physical-sciences and computer-science\nconcepts from arXiv. The MeSH population covers only biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries; its coverage rule removes 34\\% of\npartner-qualified entries, and PubMed-only entry years match all-works entry years for 50\\% of entries on the\n13 fully retrieved concepts. Generalisation to social sciences, humanities or engineering is untested.\n\n\\paragraph{Primary specification underpowered.} The fully saturated specification with concept-by-year and\nhost-by-year fixed effects, which absorbs more confounding than the co-primary, is inconclusive on the Held-out\nfold (IRR 0.98, 30 clusters). The held-out confirmation rests on the co-primary specification, which leaves\nmore residual variation; on MeSH the primary specification is significant (IRR 1.32).\n\n\\paragraph{Single-paper entries.} 87\\% of co-primary Screen events involve a single entry-year paper. The\npooled multi-team effect is positive (IRR 1.28, 95\\% CI 1.11 to 1.48), but the Held-out alone is underpowered\nfor this test.\n\n\\paragraph{Binary establishment null.} The host-vocabulary share predicts the count of newcomer papers and the\nprobability that any newcomer uptake occurs, but binary establishment (at least three newcomer papers, with host papers in at least\nthree of the five years) is null on the Held-out fold ($p = 0.165$). The effect is graded, not threshold-based.\n\n\\paragraph{Cluster-robust inference.} The cluster-robust variance estimator rejects 10\\% to 11\\% of null\nshuffles in simulation (target 5\\%; an earlier 200-draw audit reported 17.5\\%). Wild-cluster bootstrap and permutation tests give consistent results\n(Held-out wild $p = 0.012$, permutation $p = 0.026$), but the standard $p$-values should not be taken at\nface value.\n\n\\paragraph{Host-specificity caveat.} The Balassa-index lift measure used to test host-specificity has a\nwithin-fixed-effect correlation of 0.997 with the log of the continuous host-vocabulary share. The lift test\nconfirms the continuous measure rather than providing independent evidence.\n\n\\paragraph{Screen-fold adopter evidence.} The adopter-level enrichment (OR 3.09) is Screen-fold only, not\nindependently confirmed. The design cannot separate absorptive capacity from topical proximity.\n\n\\paragraph{Closure held-out caveats.} RQ1 is R1\\_DEAD under the frozen kill rule. The one confirmed row,\npersistent-neighbour closure, had a screen event-study interval that included zero, and the held-out matching\nfalls back to Screen controls for 17 of 25 unique controls, so the estimator is not fully control-side\nindependent; covariate balance is poor. The MeSH closure result is\ndirectional under the sensitivity label but null under the primary label.\n\n\\section{Conclusions}\n\\label{sec:conclusions}\n\nWhen a new scientific concept enters a disciplinary subfield, the vocabulary composition of its initial\npartners predicts whether newcomer scientists in that field will subsequently adopt it. This host-vocabulary\neffect (Screen IRR 1.30; sealed held-out IRR 1.19; MeSH co-primary IRR 1.23, verdict REPLICATED for\nbiomedicine-to-biomedicine entries) governs how much newcomer uptake follows rather than whether a binary\nestablishment threshold is crossed. It is host-specific\n--- though the Balassa-index lift leg of this test is near-collinear with the continuous share\n(within-fixed-effect $r = 0.997$) --- operates through both the extensive and intensive margins, and does\nnot vary by the concept's origin field. Co-transfer of origin companions is null.\n\nFor emergence, the answer is negative: structural precursors of sustained uptake are volume/churn\ncorrelates (R1\\_DEAD under the frozen kill rule). Persistent-neighbour closure is lower before sustained uptake on\nthe held-out fold (panel coefficient $-1.07$, Holm $p = 0.015$; event-study standardised mean difference\n$-0.83$, 95\\% CI $[-1.71, -0.10]$), but it is a single qualified row. Burt constraint is higher, so the\nincreasing-brokerage pathway is ruled out for emerging concepts.\n\nThese results bear on how knowledge transfer is evaluated and supported. Policies and platforms that facilitate\ncross-disciplinary research might benefit from attending to the vocabulary composition of a concept's first\nappearance in a new field, rather than only to the mobility of authors who carry it.\n\nFuture work should extend the concept pool beyond the physical and computational sciences, test whether the\nhost-vocabulary gradient holds for social-science and humanities concepts, and design an experiment to separate\nabsorptive capacity from topical proximity at the adopter level.\n\n\\section*{Declarations}\n\n\\paragraph{Availability of data and materials.} All data derive from OpenAlex, an open scholarly metadata\nindex. The concept pool, verified work lists and analysis code are available in the project repository at\n\\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new}.\n\n\\paragraph{Competing interests.} No competing interests are declared.\n\n\\paragraph{Funding.} Not applicable.\n\n\\paragraph{Authors' contributions.} Not applicable.\n\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "numLines": 808, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 808}}

Burt constraint is positive: emerging concepts sit in more constrained, not more brokered, ego networks.</p>\n378:    <p>A stable <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/experiment-8\">two-type typology</a> (localised vs. broad from the start), an expansion-before-diffusion ordering (25 of 26 dual-onset concepts), and <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/evaluation-5\">adopter enrichment</a> for prior partner exposure (OR 3.09; prevalence 0.79 vs.&nbsp;0.61; screen fold only).</p>\n379:    <p class=\"code-links\">Code: <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/evaluation-4\">Checking concept spread types on unseen and medical data</a></p>\n398:<p>The <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-1/dataset-1\">concept pool</a> contains 426 scientific concepts (366 emerging, 60 stationary reference) that first appeared in OpenAlex between 2005 and 2016, with 20 to 300 first-appearance papers. Of the 366 emerging concepts, 247 form the screen fold and 119 the held-out fold, split by a SHA-1 hash before any outcomes were inspected. Each concept was <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-1\">grounded</a> through a logistic-regression classifier (F1&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.82, AUC&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.89) and variant merger (B-cubed F1&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.78). An independent check population of <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-1/dataset-3\">191 new MeSH biomedical concepts</a> was drawn from MeSH descriptors established 2004 to 2018.</p>\n401:<p>From a design-weighted background sample of 259,716 works, the study built 25 yearly three-year-window <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-3\">co-occurrence snapshots</a> (approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges per snapshot) with association-strength edge weights and Leiden community detection.</p>\n416:<p>On the screen fold, a one-standard-deviation increase in host-vocabulary share raises newcomer uptake by 30% (co-primary IRR 1.30, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.45). On the sealed <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/evaluation-2\">held-out fold</a>, opened once, the co-primary IRR is 1.19 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.33; the pre-declared kill rule is not triggered). On the <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/experiment-9\">MeSH biomedical population</a>, the co-primary IRR is 1.23 (95% CI 1.12 to 1.36; verdict REPLICATED for biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries). The inverse-variance weighted pooled estimate across screen and MeSH is 1.26 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.36).</p>\n422:<p>The host-vocabulary effect operates through both margins. The <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-5/evaluation-6\">extensive-margin</a> effect is +6.4 percentage points per standard deviation (95% CI 4.8 to 8.1), approximately a 13% increase relative to the 51% base rate. The intensive-margin IRR per standard deviation is 1.18 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.27). The extensive margin accounts for 38% of the total effect (95% CI 21% to 55%); the intensive margin accounts for the remaining 62%.</p>\n427:<p>Newcomer scientists who adopt a concept are enriched for prior corpus exposure to its <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-4/evaluation-5\">entry partners</a> (conditional logistic regression OR 3.09; prevalence 0.79 vs.&nbsp;0.61; 1,013 matched strata, screen fold only, not independently confirmed). Enrichment follows a vocabulary gradient: FOREIGN partners OR 2.88, ADJACENT partners OR 1.91, NATIVE partners OR 1.47. The design cannot separate absorptive capacity from topical proximity.</p>\n432:<p>Under the pre-registered kill rule, R1_DEAD: structural precursors of sustained uptake are volume and churn correlates. Only <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/experiment-5\">persistent-neighbour closure</a> survives Holm correction on the held-out fold (panel coefficient &minus;1.07, Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.015; event-study standardised mean difference &minus;0.83, 95% CI [&minus;1.71, &minus;0.10]). General closure (Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.147) and turnover-residualised closure (Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.635) do not survive. Burt constraint is positive (+0.11, 95% CI [0.02, 0.19]): emerging concepts sit in more constrained, not more brokered, ego networks.</p>\n433:<p>The <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-4\">MeSH closure replication</a> is directional under a sensitivity label (standardised mean difference &minus;0.42, Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.039, n&nbsp;=&nbsp;29) but null under the primary label (&minus;0.09, Holm p&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.677, n&nbsp;=&nbsp;15).</p>\n438:<p>Co-transfer is null in all specifications and populations. The <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/experiment-6\">breadth-prediction screen</a> (does openness predict how many new subfields a concept will reach?) found no effect beyond growth and level baselines. The link between pre-emergence closure and later host-entry vocabulary composition is null (partial correlation 0.025 screen, 0.053 held-out, both intervals including zero).</p>\n506:  <li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-1/dataset-4\">Labelled science phrases and new-term pool</a></li>\n507:  <li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-1/research-1\">Prior art and plan for concept-spread study</a></li>\n508:  <li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-2/experiment-2\">Do concept citation chains survive in new fields?</a></li>\n509:  <li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-3/evaluation-1\">Checking the report's numbers and the closure effect</a></li>\n510:  <li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-5/evaluation-8\">Check every paper number against its source</a></li>\n511:  <li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-5/research-2\">Where the host-vocabulary finding sits in the literature</a></li>\n512:  <li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/round-5/evaluation-9\">Paper figures drawn straight from result files</a></li>\n519:  <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/paper.pdf\">Read the paper (PDF)</a>", "stderr": "", "interrupted": false, "isImage": false, "noOutputExpected": false}

<a class="skip" href="#main">Skip to main content</a>
<header class="hero" id="top">
  <p class="kicker">Interactive companion to the paper</p>
  <h1>Host vocabulary predicts whether new scientific concepts take root across disciplinary boundaries</h1>
  <p class="byline">Pre-registered study of 426 OpenAlex concepts and 191 MeSH concepts. The paper lists no author line.</p>
  <p class="links">
    <a class="btn primary" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/paper.pdf">Read the paper (PDF)</a>
    <a class="btn" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA/report.pdf">Read the full research report</a>
    <a class="btn" href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_MvbsSpVmwUlA">Code repository</a>
  </p>
</header>
<nav class="toc" aria-label="Sections">
  <ul>
    <li><a href="#finding">The finding</a></li>
    <li><a href="#how">How it works</a></li>
    <li><a href="#explore">Explore the evidence</a></li>
    <li><a href="#try">Try a threshold</a></li>
    <li><a href="#fails">Where it fails</a></li>
    <li><a href="#about">Sources and glossary</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>
<main id="main">

<section class="block" id="finding" aria-labelledby="h-finding">
  <h2 id="h-finding">The finding</h2>
  <div class="grid2">
    <div class="prose">
      <p class="q"><strong>The question.</strong> When a scientific concept first shows up in a subfield outside its origin, what decides whether researchers in that subfield take it up?</p>
      <p>Each such arrival is a <button class="term" data-term="hostentry">host-entry event</button>. The paper measures the <button class="term" data-term="share">host-vocabulary share</button> of the partner terms the concept arrives with, and asks whether it predicts <button class="term" data-term="uptake">newcomer uptake</button> over the next five years.</p>
      <p><strong>The answer.</strong> It does. On the sealed <button class="term" data-term="heldout">held-out fold</button>, opened once, one standard deviation more host vocabulary goes with this much more newcomer uptake:</p>
      <p class="bignum" id="bignum" aria-describedby="bignum-cap"></p>
      <p class="bignum-cap" id="bignum-cap"></p>
      <p>The <button class="term" data-term="ct">co-transfer</button> of origin companions, the natural competitor, is null on every fold. The chart draws both regressors from the pre-registered <button class="term" data-term="ppml">PPML</button> models. Switch the specification to see the stricter <button class="term" data-term="primary">primary</button> model, which is inconclusive on the held-out fold.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="card">
      <h3 style="margin-top:0">Does it hold on every fold?</h3>
      <div class="controls">
        <fieldset>
          <legend>Specification</legend>
          <div class="seg" role="radiogroup" aria-label="Specification">
            <label><input type="radio" name="f-spec" value="co" checked><span>Co-primary</span></label>
            <label><input type="radio" name="f-spec" value="pri"><span>Primary (strict FE)</span></label>
          </div>
        </fieldset>
        <label class="chk"><input type="checkbox" id="f-ct" checked> Show co-transfer rows</label>
      </div>
      <div class="chart" id="c-forest"></div>
      <ul class="legend" aria-label="Legend">
        <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>Host-vocabulary share, OpenAlex folds</li>
        <li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--green)"></span>Host-vocabulary share, MeSH</li>
        <li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--amber);transform:rotate(45deg)"></span>IVW pool</li>
        <li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--muted);transform:rotate(45deg)"></span>Co-transfer</li>
        <li><span class="sw dash"></span>IRR = 1, no effect</li>
      </ul>
      <p class="takeaway" id="t-forest" aria-live="polite"></p>
      <p class="note">Values: incidence-rate ratio per SD with 95% concept-clustered CI. Source: the run's figure registry (evaluation 9, <code>figures/F2/plotted_values.json</code>).</p>

  </div>
</section>

<section class="block" id="how" aria-labelledby="h-how">
  <h2 id="h-how">How it works: one real entry, stage by stage</h2>
  <p class="q"><strong>How does a concept's arrival become a number in the regression?</strong> Follow Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen (EPR) steering, a quantum-physics concept, as it enters the OpenAlex subfield labelled Artificial Intelligence in 2011. Every value below is the one the run recorded for this entry.</p>
  <div class="card" id="stepper" tabindex="-1" aria-roledescription="stepper">
    <div class="chart pipe" id="c-pipe" aria-label="Method pipeline"></div>
    <div class="stepnav">
      <button class="b" id="s-prev" type="button">Previous</button>
      <button class="b" id="s-next" type="button">Next</button>
      <span class="note" id="s-count"></span>
    </div>
    <p class="sr" aria-live="polite" id="s-live"></p>
    <h3 id="s-title" style="margin-top:6px"></h3>
    <div class="stagebox">
      <div><h4>What goes in</h4><div id="s-in"></div></div>
      <div><h4>What is done</h4><div id="s-do"></div></div>
      <div><h4>What comes out</h4><div id="s-out"></div></div>
    </div>
    <p id="s-why" class="prose"></p>
    <div class="chart" id="c-stage"></div>
    <p class="note">Use the Previous and Next buttons, click a stage in the diagram, or press the left and right arrow keys while the stepper has focus.</p>
  </div>
  <figure>
    <img src="figures/fig1_v0.jpg" width="3840" height="1648" loading="lazy" alt="Study design in four panels: (a) the arXiv concept pool of 426 concepts split into screen and held-out folds, plus the 191-concept MeSH population, drawn from 462,812 OpenAlex works; (b) a co-word network with three colour-coded Leiden communities; (c) a schematic matched event study comparing a concept with sustained uptake to a flat control; (d) a concept moving from its origin subfield into a host subfield, where host-native and origin partner terms feed the host-vocabulary share used to predict five-year newcomer uptake.">
    <figcaption>Figure 1 of the paper. Overview of the study design. (a) Data: an outcome-blind arXiv concept pool of 426 emerging scientific concepts, split into a screen fold (247) and a held-out fold (119), and an independent MeSH biomedical check population of 191 concepts. Both are drawn from 462,812 OpenAlex works. (b) Co-word network: yearly co-word snapshots (25 snapshots, ~27k nodes, ~84k edges) with Leiden communities; the schematic shows three colour-coded communities. (c) RQ1, emergence precursors: a matched event study compares closure measures in the pre-onset window (shaded) between concepts showing sustained uptake (blue, rising after onset) and controls (grey, flat). (d) RQ2, host-entry grafting: a concept enters a non-origin host subfield (light blue → light green region). Its partner terms are either host-native (dark green) or from the origin vocabulary (light blue). The host-vocabulary share (orange) is the exposure in a pre-registered PPML regression with concept-clustered standard errors predicting 5-year newcomer uptake. The timelines and bars in (c) and (d) are schematic and carry no data values.</figcaption>
  </figure>
</section>

<section class="block" id="explore" aria-labelledby="h-explore">
  <h2 id="h-explore">Explore the evidence</h2>

  <h3 id="h-bins">Across all recorded entries, does uptake rise with host-vocabulary share?</h3>
  <p class="q">The regression holds concept, entry year and host fixed. This view drops all of that and simply sorts every recorded entry of a fold by its host-vocabulary share, cuts the list into equal-sized groups and averages the outcome in each group.</p>
  <div class="card">
    <div class="controls">
      <label>Fold <select id="b-fold"></select></label>
      <label>Groups <select id="b-bins"><option value="4">4 (quartiles)</option><option value="5" selected>5 (quintiles)</option><option value="10">10 (deciles)</option></select></label>
      <fieldset>
        <legend>Outcome</legend>
        <div class="seg" role="radiogroup" aria-label="Outcome">
          <label><input type="radio" name="b-metric" value="mean" checked><span>Mean newcomer papers</span></label>
          <label><input type="radio" name="b-metric" value="any"><span>Share with any uptake</span></label>
        </div>
      </fieldset>
    </div>
    <div class="chart" id="c-bins"></div>
    <ul class="legend"><li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>Group of entries, lowest to highest share</li><li><span class="sw dash"></span>Fold average (baseline)</li></ul>
    <p class="takeaway" id="t-bins" aria-live="polite"></p>
    <p class="note">Computed in the page from the per-entry records. These are raw averages with no fixed effects or controls, so they describe the data and are not the paper's estimate. The Screen fold holds all 1,740 recorded entries with at least five partners (the co-primary model keeps 1,544); Held-out holds 1,097 (model keeps 972); MeSH holds 2,249 (model keeps 2,171).</p>
  </div>

  <h3 id="h-browser">What happened to one entry?</h3>
  <p class="q">Pick any recorded host entry. The panel puts its inputs beside two model predictions of its newcomer papers, one from the controls-only model and one with host-vocabulary share and co-transfer added, and beside what was observed.</p>
  <div class="card">
    <div class="controls">
      <label>Fold <select id="r-fold"></select></label>
      <label>Search <input type="search" id="r-q" placeholder="concept or host subfield" aria-describedby="r-count"></label>
      <label>Show <select id="r-filter">
        <option value="all">All entries</option>
        <option value="any">Any newcomer uptake</option>
        <option value="none">No newcomer uptake</option>
        <option value="est">Established (Screen and MeSH only)</option>
      </select></label>
      <label>Sort by <select id="r-sort">
        <option value="share">Host-vocabulary share, high to low</option>
        <option value="y">Newcomer papers, high to low</option>
        <option value="resid">Observed minus predicted, high to low</option>
        <option value="year">Entry year</option>
      </select></label>
    </div>
    <p class="note" id="r-count" aria-live="polite"></p>

      <div>
        <div class="tablewrap">
          <table>
            <caption class="sr">Recorded host-entry events</caption>
            <thead><tr><th scope="col">Concept</th><th scope="col">Host subfield</th><th scope="col" class="num">Year</th><th scope="col" class="num">Share</th><th scope="col" class="num">Newcomer papers</th></tr></thead>
            <tbody id="r-body"></tbody>
          </table>
        </div>
        <p><button class="b" id="r-more" type="button">Show 40 more</button></p>
      </div>
      <div id="r-detail" aria-live="polite">
        <h4 id="d-title"></h4>
        <dl class="kv" id="d-kv"></dl>
        <div class="chart" id="c-pred"></div>
        <ul class="legend"><li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--muted)"></span>Controls-only model</li><li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>With host-vocabulary share and co-transfer</li><li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--ink)"></span>Observed</li></ul>
        <h4 style="margin-top:16px" id="d-sib-title">Other entries of this concept in this fold</h4>

        <p class="takeaway" id="t-detail"></p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <p class="note">Predictions: Screen and MeSH use grouped out-of-fold Poisson predictions recorded by the run (experiment 7, experiment 9). Held-out uses the Screen-fitted models applied to the sealed fold (evaluation 2). They are descriptive checks, not the inferential test.</p>
  </div>

  <h3 id="h-margins">Does host vocabulary start uptake, or make it larger?</h3>
  <p class="q">The effect splits into an <button class="term" data-term="extensive">extensive margin</button> (whether any newcomer uptake starts) and an <button class="term" data-term="intensive">intensive margin</button> (how much, once it has started). This decomposition was frozen after the confirmation and is exploratory.</p>

    </div>

    <p class="note">Source: evaluation 6, <code>results/k1_decomposition.json</code>.</p>
  </div>

  <h3 id="h-cases">What does the gradient look like inside one concept?</h3>
  <p class="q">Four medoid concepts from the typology. Each bar is one host entry, sorted by host-vocabulary share; green bars are entries that took root.</p>
  <div class="card">
    <div class="tabs" role="tablist" aria-label="Case concept" id="k-tabs"></div>

    <p class="takeaway" id="t-cases" aria-live="polite"></p>

</section>

<section class="block" id="try" aria-labelledby="h-try">
  <h2 id="h-try">Try it: call an entry host-leaning above a threshold</h2>
  <p class="q">The model uses the share as a continuous number. What if you split entries at a cut-off instead? Drag the threshold and the page recomputes, from the recorded entries, how often each side attracted any newcomer and how many newcomer papers it drew.</p>
  <div class="card">
    <div class="controls">
      <label>Fold <select id="w-fold"></select></label>
      <label for="w-th">Threshold on host-vocabulary share</label>
      <input type="range" id="w-th" min="0" max="0.2" step="0.005" value="0.05" aria-describedby="w-thv">
      <output id="w-thv" for="w-th"></output>
      <fieldset>
        <legend>Bar shows</legend>
        <div class="seg" role="radiogroup" aria-label="Bar shows">
          <label><input type="radio" name="w-metric" value="any" checked><span>Share with any uptake</span></label>
          <label><input type="radio" name="w-metric" value="mean"><span>Mean newcomer papers</span></label>
        </div>
      </fieldset>
    </div>
    <div class="stats" id="w-stats"></div>
    <div class="chart" id="c-whatif"></div>
    <ul class="legend"><li><span class="sw sq" style="background:#b8bec6"></span>Below the threshold</li><li><span class="sw sq" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>At or above the threshold</li></ul>
    <p class="takeaway" id="t-whatif" aria-live="polite"></p>
    <p class="note">Raw comparison with no controls. The paper's model does not use a cut-off: only 1.1% of partner tags have a host share above 50%, which is why the continuous share is primary, and binary nativeness cut-offs at 0.5 and 0.7 are null. A PPML with concept, year and host fixed effects cannot be refitted honestly in a browser, so this view sweeps a threshold over the recorded outcomes instead.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<section class="block" id="fails" aria-labelledby="h-fails">
  <h2 id="h-fails">Where it fails</h2>
  <h3>Which entries go against the gradient?</h3>
  <p class="q">A graded effect leaves plenty of exceptions. Pick a kind of exception and a fold; the counts come from the recorded entries.</p>
  <div class="card">
    <div class="controls">
      <label>Fold <select id="x-fold"></select></label>
      <fieldset>
        <legend>Exception</legend>
        <div class="seg" role="radiogroup" aria-label="Exception">
          <label><input type="radio" name="x-kind" value="hinone" checked><span>Top-decile share, no uptake</span></label>
          <label><input type="radio" name="x-kind" value="lohigh"><span>Bottom-half share, 10+ newcomer papers</span></label>
        </div>
      </fieldset>
    </div>
    <div class="stats" id="x-stats"></div>
    <ul class="faillist" id="x-list"></ul>
    <p class="takeaway" id="t-fails" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </div>

  <h3>The emergence question returned dead</h3>
  <p class="q">The paper's second question (RQ1) asked whether network structure before take-off marks the concepts that later show <button class="term" data-term="eup">sustained uptake</button>. The held-out test, under its frozen kill rule, returned <button class="term" data-term="r1dead">R1_DEAD</button>. Switch estimator and fold to see which closure rows survive.</p>
  <div class="card">
    <div class="controls">
      <fieldset>
        <legend>Estimator</legend>
        <div class="seg" role="radiogroup" aria-label="Estimator">
          <label><input type="radio" name="c-est" value="pp" checked><span>Pooled panel</span></label>
          <label><input type="radio" name="c-est" value="es"><span>Matched event study</span></label>
        </div>
      </fieldset>
      <fieldset>
        <legend>Fold</legend>
        <div class="seg" role="radiogroup" aria-label="Fold">
          <label><input type="radio" name="c-fold" value="ho" checked><span>Held-out</span></label>
          <label><input type="radio" name="c-fold" value="scr"><span>Screen</span></label>
        </div>
      </fieldset>
    </div>
    <div class="chart" id="c-closure"></div>
    <ul class="legend"><li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--accent)"></span>Confirmed on held-out</li><li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--muted)"></span>Not confirmed</li><li><span class="sw" style="background:var(--amber)"></span>Burt constraint (positive)</li><li><span class="sw dash"></span>No difference</li></ul>
    <p class="takeaway" id="t-closure" aria-live="polite"></p>
    <p class="note">Measures: <button class="term" data-term="persist">persistent-neighbour closure</button>, <button class="term" data-term="burt">Burt constraint</button>. Values are rounded to two decimals from the figure registry's three-decimal values (evaluation 9, <code>figures/F4/plotted_values.json</code>, drawn from evaluation 3). <button class="term" data-term="holm">Holm</button> p-values test the held-out panel coefficient.</p>
  </div>

  <h3>What the paper does not show</h3>
  <ul class="lim">
    <li><strong>The strict model is inconclusive on held-out.</strong> With concept-by-year and host-by-year fixed effects, the held-out IRR is 0.98 (95% CI 0.70 to 1.37) on 250 of 972 events and 30 clusters, declared underpowered in advance. The held-out confirmation rests on the co-primary specification.</li>
    <li><strong>Graded, not a threshold.</strong> Binary establishment (at least three newcomer papers, with host papers in at least three of the five years) is null on the held-out fold (p = 0.165).</li>
    <li><strong>Population.</strong> The pool is dominated by physics and computer-science concepts from arXiv. The MeSH replication covers biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries only. Social sciences, humanities and engineering are untested.</li>
    <li><strong>What the held-out fold protects.</strong> Its outcomes were sealed and opened once, but its entry events, pre-entry features and size came from the same pipeline, and an early experiment computed origin-series summaries for 61 of its concepts.</li>
    <li><strong>Single-paper entries.</strong> 87% of co-primary Screen events involve a single entry-year paper. The pooled multi-team effect is positive (IRR 1.28, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.48); the held-out fold alone is underpowered for this test.</li>
    <li><strong>Inference.</strong> The cluster-robust variance estimator rejects 10% to 11% of null shuffles in simulation (target 5%). Wild-cluster bootstrap and permutation tests agree with the held-out result (wild p = 0.012, permutation p = 0.026).</li>
    <li><strong>Host-specificity.</strong> The Balassa-index lift measure has a within-fixed-effect correlation of 0.997 with the log of the continuous share, so it confirms the share rather than adding independent evidence.</li>
    <li><strong>Adopters.</strong> Adopters are enriched for prior exposure to the entry partners (OR 3.09; prevalence 0.79 vs. 0.61), on the Screen fold only. The design cannot separate absorptive capacity from topical proximity.</li>
    <li><strong>Closure.</strong> The one confirmed closure row had a screen event-study interval that included zero, 17 of 25 held-out controls are screen concepts, and covariate balance is poor.</li>
  </ul>
</section>
